query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated Mn content (exceeding ~15 at.%) in CrFeCoNiX HEAs drives rapid outward Mn diffusion, resulting in the formation of a thick, porous, and unstable Mn-rich oxide scale that is prone to cracking and spallation during oxidation at temperatures >900 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy with Mn content deliberately increased to over 15 at.% (verified by compositional analysis).
generation.intervention: Fabricate alloy variants with controlled Mn concentrations (one with ≥15 at.% Mn versus a baseline with reduced Mn achieved by partial substitution with a more refractory element such as Al), while keeping other elements constant.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloys to an oxidizing atmosphere (air) at approximately 950 °C for 48 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Excess Mn, due to its high diffusivity, leads to the formation of a thick oxide layer predominantly composed of Mn2O3/Mn3O4, which is porous and mechanically weak.
generation.mechanism: High Mn content beyond a critical threshold accelerates Mn oxidation so that rapid outward diffusion produces a porous, loosely adherent oxide network. Interactions with Cr and Fe are insufficient in compensating for the instability, causing cracks and subsequent spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-Mn alloy will develop oxide scales that are >20 µm thick with visible porosity, cracks, and spallation, whereas the baseline alloy (with reduced Mn) will exhibit a more stable, less thick oxide layer.
generation.baseline: A comparable CrFeCoNiX alloy where Mn is reduced by partial substitution with an element that decreases overall Mn diffusivity.
generation.boundary: Applicable to single-phase HEAs oxidized in air at temperatures >900 °C over ~48 hours, with composition as the controlled variable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of ~15 at.% Mn is derived from current literature and may vary with interactions with Cr and Fe; further quantitative kinetic studies are required to refine this value.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two alloy variants differing only in Mn content (e.g., one with ≥15 at.% Mn and another with reduced Mn via partial substitution). Expose both to air at 950 °C for 48 hours.
measurements: SEM/TEM cross-sectional imaging for oxide morphology and thickness
XRD and EDS analyses to identify oxide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Mn (≥15 at.%) alloy does not exhibit a significantly thicker, more porous, and less adherent oxide scale compared to the lower-Mn baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

This phenomenon is closely linked to the differential diffusion rates of the multi-principal elements within the Cantor alloy. Based on the findings reported by Tsai et al. [] and Kai et al. [], the order of elements in terms of the decreasing diffusion rate is as follows: Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni. The initialisation and evolution of different oxide phases that were found with XRD scans agree well with these elements’ diffusion sequence order. Mn, Cr, and Fe preferentially diffused outward and became oxidized on the surface of specimens with time and temperature. Furthermore, as the temperature increases, it becomes apparent that the substrate’s FCC phase diminishes, likely due to the concurrent increase in oxide layer thickness, which consequently leads to a weakening of the peak intensity associated with the FCC phase []. No protective oxide-like Cr2O3 formed; instead, MnCr2O4 formed at 800 °C, adding to the already identified Mn2O3 oxide formed at 700 °C. Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Multi‐element HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn, with possible substitutions by Al or Si) in oxidizing environments above 900 °C.
papers.approach: Combined in situ atom probe tomography (APT), high‐resolution electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and XANES to visualize elemental distribution and track oxidation evolution; introduced the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) to predict surface speciation.
papers.findings: Observed that at higher temperatures, oxidation evolves from early-stage atomic size-controlled behavior to redox-driven compositional inversion (TOCI) where faster-diffusing elements (e.g., Mn) form outer, often non-protective oxides, while slower diffusing elements (e.g., Cr and Al) tend to form inner layers. Under extended oxidation, segregation and island-like agglomerates develop leading to complex layered oxide structures.
papers.mechanism: Element-specific diffusion kinetics and oxidation potentials govern whether a continuous, protective oxide (e.g., Cr2O3 or Al2O3) forms. The PIP framework predicts that if the passivating element’s (Cr or Al) outward diffusion dominates and its oxide remains stable (versus volatile manganese oxides), a coherent oxide layer develops. Conversely, if a highly mobile element (Mn) dominates, unstable oxides and subsequent spallation can occur.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi HEA studied under both air and vacuum environments, with experiment temperatures up to 1100 °C.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) to monitor phase evolution and oxide formation during oxidation, supplemented by thermodynamic calculations using CALPHAD.
papers.findings: Found that at temperatures above 900 °C, Mn oxidizes rapidly, forming non-protective oxides and depleting the alloy’s Mn content; layered oxide structures with outer Mn-rich and inner Cr-rich regions were observed. No distinct protective Cr2O3 was detected in some cases, contrasting with earlier studies.
papers.mechanism: The differential diffusion rates (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni) lead to the preferential oxidation of less-protective species (Mn) at the surface. The interplay between outward cation diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion determines the layered oxide structure. Volatility issues (e.g., formation of CrO3 at high temperatures) may further destabilize protective Cr oxides.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X HEAs where Mn is partially substituted by Al (X = varying from Si, Mn to Al compositions).
papers.approach: Experimental study using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering to fabricate alloys with varying Al content; oxidation tests were performed including prolonged isothermal annealing at elevated temperatures.
papers.findings: Increasing Al content leads to a transformation in the outer oxide composition from Mn-based oxides to a dense, ultrathin, and protective AlxOy scale. Alloys with higher Al showed suppressed internal oxidation and absence of spallation compared to those rich in Mn.
papers.mechanism: The formation of a coherent, protective alumina scale is attributed to the lower diffusivity of Al and the slower, more controlled oxidation kinetics of Al2O3 relative to Mn-oxides. In contrast, a high Mn content accelerates porous oxide growth that cracks and spalls.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.system: Equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi HEA, modeled both as a homogeneous single-crystal and with dendritic-core/interdendritic microstructures (representative of multiphase solid-solution states).
papers.approach: Stochastic cellular automata simulations incorporating diffusion coefficients (from molecular simulations) and reconstructed micrographs to predict mesoscale oxidation behavior and scale formation over extended times.
papers.findings: Simulations indicate that in a single-crystal system, Al2O3 and Cr2O3 form uniformly, leading to a more protective oxide scale. In multiphase structures reflecting dendritic segregation, distinct oxide clusters form (α-Al2O3-rich on Al-Ni domains and Cr2O3-rich on Cr-Fe domains), which could affect overall coherence of the protective layer.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation is controlled by both intrinsic diffusion kinetics and microstructural heterogeneity. In a homogeneous system, protective scales form by steady-state diffusion processes, while in multiphase alloys, spatially variant elemental distributions lead to non-uniform oxide initiation, challenging layer stability.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed to yield ultrafine-grain microstructures versus as-cast coarse-grained specimens.
papers.approach: Experimental investigation using controlled deformation (high strain rate processing) to refine grain sizes; oxidation kinetics were studied via thermogravimetric analysis, cross-sectional microscopy, and kinetic modeling at temperatures above 900 °C.
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grain alloys exhibit a higher density of grain boundaries that facilitate rapid formation of a continuous, protective Cr-rich oxide scale (followed by inner Al2O3) compared to coarser grained samples. This leads to lower parabolic oxidation rate constants and reduced spallation.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced intergranular diffusion in ultrafine-grained alloys promotes rapid and uniform oxide nucleation, leading to a denser and more adherent protective oxide layer. The optimized microstructural pathways thus reduce oxygen ingress and subsequent oxidation of the substrate.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co (and sometimes Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni) HEA studied at 700–900 °C under varying oxygen partial pressures.
papers.approach: Experimental oxidation tests using 3D laser printed samples combined with XRD, microscopic analysis, and oxidation kinetics measurements.
papers.findings: At 900 °C, the alloy suffers from significant oxide layer spallation and formation of non-adherent oxide phases (e.g., MnFe2O4, MnFeO2, Cr-containing spinels), although at lower temperatures (700 °C) a more adherent oxide forms. Oxidation kinetics are parabolic but degrade sharply with temperature increase.
papers.mechanism: The high-temperature oxidation behavior is governed by the competition between rapid diffusion of Mn and the slower, more stable oxidation of Cr. The absence or insufficiency of a continuous protective Cr2O3 (or Al2O3, if present) layer leads to oxide scale breakdown, partly due to thermal stresses and differential diffusion rates.

established: Different alloying elements exhibit distinct oxidation behaviors due to their inherent diffusion rates and thermodynamic stabilities; for example, Al and Cr tend to form more protective oxides compared to Mn.
Temperature above 900 °C promotes volatile oxide formation (e.g., CrO3) and accelerates diffusion processes, affecting oxide layer adherence and integrity.
Microstructure (single-phase vs. multiphase, grain size) significantly influences oxidation kinetics and the ability to form continuous protective scales.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ HTXRD and atom probe tomography to track real-time oxidation and elemental diffusion.
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided insights into phase transformations and segregation dynamics that underpin the formation of layered oxides; identified conditions under which non-protective oxides form.

approaches_tried.approach: Stochastic cellular automata modeling of oxidation in idealized (single-crystal) and heterogeneous multiphase microstructures.
approaches_tried.outcome: Simulated the growth of oxide scales and predicted the impact of microstructural heterogeneity on protective oxide formation.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled microstructural modification (ultrafine-grain processing) to enhance oxidation resistance.
approaches_tried.outcome: Experimental results showed that higher grain boundary density leads to faster and more uniform protective oxide scale formation, reducing overall oxidation rates.

mechanisms: Diffusion-controlled oxidation where the relative outward diffusion rates of alloying elements (with Mn diffusing fastest and Al/Cr more slowly) determine the oxide scale composition and stability.
The preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) framework, where local atomic environments and redox potentials dictate which element oxidizes first and forms continuous layers.
Microstructure-based pathways (grain boundary diffusion in ultrafine grains) that facilitate rapid nucleation of protective oxides.
disagreements: Certain studies report the formation of a protective Cr2O3 layer under high-temperature conditions, while others find that Mn oxidation predominates and leads to non-adherent scales, questioning the universality of Cr-based passivation.
The role of multiphase microstructures versus single-phase solid solutions in facilitating or impeding protective oxide scale formation remains debated, especially regarding oxide coherence.
open_questions: How do substitutions by Si, Mn, or Al in CrFeCoNiX HEAs specifically alter the balance between protective and non-protective oxide formation at temperatures above 900 °C?

What are the quantitative contributions of controlled microstructure (e.g., single-phase versus multiphase) and elemental diffusivity to the stability of the oxide scale during long-term oxidation or corrosion?
Under what precise exposure conditions (e.g., oxidizing vs. corrosive atmospheres) does the transition occur between protective, coherent oxides and unstable, spalled scales?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparative experiments on CrFeCoNiX HEAs with systematic variations in X (Si, Mn, Al) in both single-phase and multiphase states to isolate the effect of individual alloying elements on oxide scale stability.

Utilize combined in situ techniques (HTXRD, APT) alongside advanced modeling (cellular automata) to directly correlate PIP predictions with observed oxide structure and adherence at temperatures >900 °C.

Explore the integration of microstructural tuning (e.g., ultrafine-grain processing) with compositional adjustments to achieve a defined baseline for the formation of a protective oxide, enabling clear falsification criteria (e.g., observation of oxide spallation or non-uniform oxide growth).

directions.direction: Investigate the effect of the substituent element (X = Al, Mn, or Si) on protective oxide formation via compositional design in CrFeCoNiX HEAs.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the hypothesis by comparing elements that preferentially form stable oxides (e.g. Al2O3) versus elements (e.g. Mn) that form unstable oxides. The physics of diffusion and thermodynamic oxide stability support it, and prior studies (e.g. record PMC9692591, PMC11169556) provide evidence, making it both feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Examine the oxidation behavior differences between single-phase and multiphase solid-solution states in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
directions.assessment: Single-phase alloys are expected to yield uniform oxide formation while multiphase (segregated) alloys may produce heterogeneous, stress-laden oxides that spall. This directly addresses whether a coherent oxide forms by linking compositional uniformity to protective scale quality. Existing modeling and microscopy (e.g. PMC9498035) support this, and experiments are practicable.

directions.direction: Utilize controlled grain refinement (ultrafine-grain processing) to increase grain boundary density in CrFeCoNiX HEAs and study its effect on protective oxide nucleation.
directions.assessment: Increased grain boundary density can accelerate the diffusion of protective species (Cr, Al) to form adherent oxides. Evidence (e.g. PMC9026100) shows that ultrafine-grained samples have superior oxidation resistance, directly addressing scale integrity during high-temperature exposure. The approach is grounded in well‐known diffusion physics and is experimentally feasible.

directions.direction: Conduct an in situ mechanistic study combining high-temperature XRD and atom probe tomography to monitor diffusion kinetics and elemental depletion during oxidation.
directions.assessment: This direction implicates the diffusion kinetics and preferential interactivity (PIP) framework to directly measure the rate at which oxide‐forming elements migrate to the surface, elucidating whether the balance leads to protective (coherent) or unstable (spalling) oxides. Prior in situ work (PMC11169556, PMC10384371) supports this method and it is sufficiently informative though technically challenging.

candidates.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidizing/corrosive atmosphere (e.g. air or 20% O2 in inert gas) at temperatures above 900 °C for extended durations (e.g. 100 hours).

candidates.hypothesis: High Mn content in CrFeCoNiX HEAs induces rapid outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of a porous, unstable Mn-oxide scale that is prone to cracking and spallation at >900 °C.
